title: Hosted API demo - Chat & text generation basics (Keystone Retail)
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Keystone Retail through Hosted API chat/text generation basics: streaming, key request params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff behavior, and recommended prod settings. Customer asked about latency, cost tradeoffs, data residency, and whether they should go hosted vs dedicated for initial pilot. Agreed next steps: share pricing + security docs, SE to run benchmarks with merchant prompts, customer to share sample prompt set.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-07
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Jordan Ruiz (Redwood); Liam O'Connor, Priya Patel, Amir Khan (Keystone Retail)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Jordan is our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Liam: Good, thanks. Curious to see what you have for streaming and retries, we have a couple of latency-sensitive features.
[00:14] Jordan: Awesome. We'll start with a quick Hosted API overview then jump into chat/text generation basics - streaming, params, and retry behavior. I'll do a short demo in the console and show the SDK snippets.
[00:26] Priya: Sounds good. We're particularly interested in p95 latency and how streaming affects client UX.
[00:33] Jordan: Totally. Quick note, I'll be switching between the console and a curl/JS example; transcription might miss some code punctuation.
[00:40] (brief background chatter)
[00:48] Jordan: So the Hosted API provides /chat and /text endpoints. For chat we support streaming using chunked responses - you can render incrementally in the client which reduces Time-To-First-Token for long generations. The SDK has an event emitter for tokens.
[01:05] Liam: Is streaming TCP-based? Any differences vs websocket?
[01:09] Jordan: We support HTTP chunked streaming and WebSocket for long-lived sessions in certain SDKs. For the majority of web apps, chunked streaming over HTTPS is simplest. WebSocket reduces some overhead for high qps use cases.
[01:21] Amir: And how do we handle partial responses and finalization? If a client disconnects mid-stream, do we get a completion callback?
[01:28] Jordan: Good Q - the server emits final chunk with metadata. If a client disconnects, the request completes server-side but you won't get the final acknowledgement client-side; we log the event and include it in request traces. For retry logic we recommend idempotency keys on create requests when you need at-least-once guarantees.
[01:45] Priya: About params - what should we tune first? Temperature vs top_p? Any defaults?
[01:50] Jordan: Defaults are conservative - temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95 typically. For deterministic output, lower temperature (0-0.3) and smaller top_p. max_tokens caps cost; set stop sequences to prevent runaways. We also have a response_length hint to optimize runtime.
[02:08] Maya: And from an ops perspective, batching and prefix caching can help reduce token cost for high-throughput workloads. Redwood Optimize will recommend batching config and caching for repeated prefixes.
[02:18] Liam: Can you give an example where caching helped?
[02:21] Jordan: Sure - e.g., when you have a common system prompt or repeated context like product catalogion data, prefix KV cache can save the cost of re-encoding those tokens each call. We saw 20-40% token cost reduction in similar retail workloads.
[02:35] (background typing)
[02:43] Jordan: Now I'll demo streaming in the console. (screen share noise) - okay, calling the /chat endpoint with streaming:true. You see tokens arrive in chunks; front-end shows partial sentences while model generates remaining text.
[03:05] Priya: UI looks smooth. If we have progressive rendering, customers get visible progress even for higher-latency generations.
[03:12] Jordan: Exactly. And for retries we recommend exponential backoff with jitter. Redwood's client SDK has built-in retry middleware that respects idempotency keys. For non-idempotent actions you probably want to surface errors to users rather than retrying.
[03:28] Liam: What about duplicate responses if network flakiness triggers retry?
[03:31] Jordan: That's where idempotency-key header is useful - server will dedupe duplicate requests within a sliding window. For streaming particularly, retries typically re-issue the full request unless you use resumable sessions - currently that is supported in websocket/long-poll flows.
[03:47] Amir: Latency numbers - any ballpark p95 for small chat completions? We're aiming for sub-200ms TTF for short prompts.
[03:55] Jordan: On Hosted, p50 for short prompts is ~60-90ms on our curated smallest models; p95 varies by model and sequence length - ballpark p95 for short responses is 180-400ms. We can run a benchmark with your prompts to get accurate numbers.
[04:10] Priya: And cost per token - how do we measure and optimize?
[04:14] Maya: Cost is tokens in + tokens out. Redwood Console shows token-level breakdown per request; Optimize suggests quantization/model swaps and batching to lower unit costs. For pilot most customers start on hosted, then move to dedicated if they need consistent throughput or lower marginal cost.
[04:29] Liam: We have data residency concerns - can hosted meet GDPR/UK regs?
[04:33] Maya: Hosted supports region-based routing; data at rest encryption and SOC2. For stronger residency/isolation, our Dedicated or Private options allow VPC and on-prem deployments. We'll attach our security pack with details.
[04:45] (short silence)
[04:49] Jordan: Quick demo of retry behavior via SDK - triggering a simulated 503, SDK retries twice with exponential backoff, final error surfaced. You can configure retry counts and backoff in the client.
[05:03] Priya: Is there an event stream we can hook to for observability?
[05:06] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Console captures per-request traces, latency, token counts, and can stream logs to your SIEM. We also provide webhooks for usage events.
[05:16] Liam: Any gotchas around streaming and mobile clients with flaky networks?
[05:20] Jordan: For flaky networks, resumable websocket sessions are better; for chunked HTTP, implement client-side checkpointing and idempotency so re-requests don't create duplicates. Also set shorter timeouts on the client to surface failures to users faster.
[05:34] Maya: We also recommend a fallback policy - e.g., if response latency exceeds threshold, degrade to a cached snippet or smaller model. Redwood routing can auto-fallback to cheaper model variants.
[05:45] Amir: For pilot we'd want to test with 50 qps sustained, bursts to 200 qps. Any hosted limits?
[05:51] Maya: Hosted has default quotas but we can bump them for pilots; Dedicated is recommended for sustained high throughput with predictable cost. We can provision burst capacity for Hosted during pilot.
[06:04] (brief side conversation about procurement)
[06:12] Jordan: One more note on streaming: tokens arrive with small metadata fields - token index, role, and whether it's final. Occasionally transcription picks up 'role' as 'roll' - sorry :).
[06:25] Priya: lol no worries. About function/tool calling - does Hosted support structured outputs?
[06:30] Jordan: Yes, we support function calling and structured output hints; you can request JSON schema enforcement and Redwood will attempt to format output accordingly. There's a validation layer you can enable to catch malformed JSON.
[06:44] Liam: Great. Any sample latency/cost spreadsheet you can share?
[06:47] Maya: We'll attach a benchmarking template and previous retail example. Jordan will run a bench and populate numbers with your prompts.
[06:54] (15min into call)
[15:12] Jordan: Back to retry semantics - for streaming we generally don't do partial-attempt retries automatically; we treat streaming as single transaction unless using resumable sessions.
[15:28] Priya: Understood. Do you have recommended settings for short answer FAQs vs long generative responses?
[15:33] Jordan: For FAQs, lower temperature and short max_tokens; for long generation, stream + progressive rendering, higher max_tokens but set stop sequences. Also consider truncating history and using embedding-based retrieval for context to keep prompt size down.
[20:05] Liam: How does Redwood measure tokens? Any difference vs other vendors?
[20:10] Jordan: Tokenization is model-dependent; Redwood Console normalizes token count display and maps to cost units. We include clear breakdown of input vs output tokens.
[24:47] (customer asks about SSO + audit logs)
[24:51] Maya: We support SSO (SAML/OIDC), RBAC, and audit logs. For Private deployments you can integrate with your KMS. We'll include SOC2 and architecture docs.
[30:02] Amir: If we start hosted pilot and later move to Dedicated, how seamless is model/version pinning?
[30:09] Jordan: Seamless - same API surface. You can pin model versions in your route config and do canary rollouts. Data routing rules can shift traffic between hosted and dedicated.
[33:15] Priya: Any advice on retry windows for idempotency dedupe?
[33:20] Jordan: We recommend a dedupe window of ~60s for user-facing actions, extendable for long-running jobs. Idempotency keys should be unique per user-action.
[36:00] Liam: Ok let's recap and next steps.
[36:05] Maya: Recap: we demoed streaming and SDK retries, discussed tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), caching/batching optimizations, security/residency options, and pilot sizing. Action items: we'll send pricing/security pack; Jordan will run bench; Liam will share prompts.
[36:25] Amir: That works. We'll target a pilot start in two weeks.
[36:31] Liam: Yep. Also please include a sample integration snippet for node/react.
[36:35] Maya: Will do.
[36:39] (closing chatter)
[36:45] Maya: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up by email.
[36:50] Jordan: Thanks, bye.

Notes about transcript quality: Some product names transcribed imperfectly (e.g., 'KV cache' may appear as 'k v cash'). There are occasional dropped punctuation and speaker overlaps.
